title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 8: Limits of Presidential Power
keywords: within the penumbra of the Charter
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) -- CJP's August 23, 2009 Inquirer column correcting the loose talk of 'emergency rule' and explaining, through David v. Arroyo (2006), the constitutional limits of presidential power

The precise distinction he draws: GMA did not impose 'emergency rule' on February 24, 2006; she issued PP 1017 'declaring a State of National Emergency' -- a different thing -- directing the AFP to suppress lawless violence, to enforce laws and decrees 'promulgated by me,' and to take over public utilities

The David v. Arroyo anatomy of the three powers: the valid 'call out' power (but not to justify warrantless arrests, assembly bans, or media censorship); the limited 'take care' power (only laws relevant to lawless violence, not unrelated statutes, and no Marcos-style decrees); and the 'take over' power, which the Court held belongs to Congress, not the President, absent a delegating law

His own concurring opinion as Chief Justice in David v. Arroyo -- the 'playing with fire... burn down the country' warning and the plea that the President be kept 'within the penumbra of the Charter' -- reprised to caution that no one, 'friend or foe,' should pipe her toward 'the precipice of authoritarianism'
sub_topics: The occasion: an Inquirer article by former US Ambassador Albert del Rosario and statements by de Venecia, Avelino Cruz and Raul Gonzalez about 'emergency rule' had 'disturbed many readers'; del Rosario wrote that 'emergency rule' was 'declared... on Feb. 24, 2006' and 'lifted' by 'the ninth day'

The precision correction: GMA did NOT impose 'emergency rule'; she issued Presidential Proclamation 1017 'declaring a State of National Emergency,' directing the AFP (1) to prevent or suppress lawless violence, invasion or rebellion; (2) to enforce all laws and decrees 'promulgated by me personally or upon my direction'; and (3) to take over privately owned public utilities affected with public interest

The 'call out' power (David v. Arroyo, May 3, 2006, per Sandoval-Gutierrez): the President may validly summon the AFP to contain lawless violence, but PP 1017 -- not being a martial-law declaration or a habeas-corpus suspension -- cannot justify the warrantless arrest of Randy David and others, the banning of Kilusang Mayo Uno assemblies, or the censorship of media like the Daily Tribune

The 'take care' power: the President may call on the AFP to enforce only laws relevant to suppressing lawless violence, invasion or rebellion -- not unrelated statutes (customs, family relations, contracts) -- and she cannot 'enforce obedience to all laws and decrees... promulgated by me'; the Court noted this proviso was lifted from Marcos's PP 1081 and barred her from enacting Marcos-style decrees

The 'take over' power: PP 1017 purported to authorize seizing companies like Meralco, PLDT, PAL, the Inquirer and ABS-CBN (Gonzalez confirmed the intent on ANC), but the Court struck this down -- the takeover of public utilities is an emergency power granted to Congress, not the President, and Congress 'has not so delegated' it

The summary of limits: the President may declare a national emergency and call out the military for lawless violence/invasion/rebellion, but without an enabling law she cannot (1) issue decrees, (2) command the AFP to enforce unrelated laws, or (3) take over private utilities; the 'brazen attempt to smuggle extraneous powers tainted an otherwise valid exercise of executive power'

CJP's David v. Arroyo concurrence reprised: 'Some of those who drafted PP 1017 may be testing the outer limits of presidential prerogative... They are playing with fire, and unless prudently restrained, they may one day wittingly or unwittingly burn down the country'

The historical caution: that the country 'would never have had to experience the wrenching pain of dictatorship' had the Court then had 'the moral courage to remind' a 'past President' (Marcos) of his mortality and the 'historical damnation of despots and tyrants' -- closing with the plea that no one 'whether friend or foe' pipe GMA 'into the same precipice'

notable_anecdotes: The borrowed Marcos proviso: CJP notes the Court observed that PP 1017's clause about enforcing 'all decrees... promulgated by me' was 'lifted from PP 1081' -- the very proclamation that imposed martial law in 1972 -- and so could not authorize Marcos-style decrees.

The takeover list: he recalls that PP 1017 was read to authorize seizing Meralco, PLDT, PAL, the Inquirer and ABS-CBN, with Secretary Raul Gonzalez confirming the intent on ANC -- an 'extravagant ambition' the Court struck down as a power belonging to Congress.

'Playing with fire': he quotes his own David v. Arroyo concurrence warning that those testing 'the outer limits of presidential prerogative' may 'one day wittingly or unwittingly burn down the country.'

The unlearned lesson of Marcos: he laments that the country might have been spared 'the wrenching pain of dictatorship' had the Court of that era had 'the moral courage' to remind Marcos of 'the inevitable historical damnation of despots and tyrants.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's August 23, 2009 Inquirer column, corrects the loose talk of 'emergency rule' -- prompted by former Ambassador del Rosario and others -- and uses David v. Arroyo (2006) to map the constitutional limits of presidential power. To be precise, he writes, GMA did not impose 'emergency rule' on February 24, 2006; she issued Presidential Proclamation 1017 'declaring a State of National Emergency,' directing the Armed Forces to suppress lawless violence, to enforce all laws and decrees 'promulgated by me,' and to take over public utilities. David v. Arroyo (per Sandoval-Gutierrez) then parsed three powers: the 'call out' power is valid to contain lawless violence but cannot justify the warrantless arrest of Randy David, the banning of Kilusang Mayo Uno assemblies, or the censorship of the Daily Tribune; the 'take care' power reaches only laws relevant to lawless violence (not customs, family relations or contracts) and cannot authorize Marcos-style decrees -- the Court noting that the offending proviso was 'lifted from PP 1081'; and the 'take over' power, purportedly used to threaten Meralco, PLDT, PAL, the Inquirer and ABS-CBN, belongs to Congress, not the President, who lacks any delegating law. So while the President may declare a national emergency and call out the military, without an enabling law she cannot issue decrees, enforce unrelated laws, or seize utilities -- and the 'brazen attempt to smuggle extraneous powers tainted an otherwise valid exercise of executive power.' CJP closes by reprising his own concurrence as Chief Justice: those drafting such proclamations 'are playing with fire, and unless prudently restrained, they may one day wittingly or unwittingly burn down the country,' adding that the nation might have been spared 'the wrenching pain of dictatorship' had the Court of Marcos's era had 'the moral courage' to remind him of 'the historical damnation of despots and tyrants' -- and pleading that no one, 'friend or foe,' pipe GMA 'into the same precipice.'
